docs.title: agenteval
docs.text:
Run your LLM agent many times, trace every step, and find out why it fails.

An agent that answers well in a demo can still be slow, expensive, flaky, or right for the wrong reason: it answered from memory instead of using its tools, or a rate limit made half its runs fail. A single accuracy number hides all of that.

agenteval runs your agent over a set of questions, several times each, records every model call and tool call, and tells you:

  • how often it's right, overall and by kind of question;
  • why it fails: a wrong answer, a tool error, a timeout, a rate limit, a quota, an injected instruction it obeyed. Each failure is labelled with its cause;
  • how it uses its tools: the right tool, valid arguments, results it actually used;
  • what it costs and how long it takes, per correct answer and at p50/p95;
  • whether a change made it better, with a paired statistical test, so you don't ship a prompt tweak that only looked better by chance.
pip install "pyagenteval[server]"
agenteval init      # an example agent, a few questions, a config
agenteval run       # no API key needed for the example
agenteval ui        # see it in your browser

Experiment 5: groq-first   config v=c98ba11d65cb   48 trials
Model:            openai/gpt-oss-20b   dataset: mixed
Pass rate:        100.0%
Latency p50/p95:  1042ms / 57768ms total, 987ms / 1572ms excluding waits
Tool calls:
  right tool        100.0%  (48 trials)
  valid arguments   100.0%  (48 trials)
  ran without error 93.8%  (48 trials)
Retries:          1 (rate_limit 1)
Cost:             $0.0027 total, $0.000057 per success
Failures:         none

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Quickstart: your own agent evaluated in five minutes.
  • Connect your agent: plain functions, OpenAI clients, LangChain and LangGraph.
  • Compare versions and gate CI: block a pull request that makes the agent worse.
  • agenteval vs other tools: how it relates to Ragas, DeepEval and promptfoo.

Names

The project is agent-eval, the Python package and command are agenteval, and you install it from PyPI as pyagenteval.

docs.title: agenteval vs other tools
docs.text:
Tools for evaluating LLM applications overlap, but each starts from a different question. This is how agenteval relates to the better-known ones; check each project's own docs for current details.

agenteval Ragas DeepEval promptfoo Starts from "is my agent reliable, and is this version better?" "is this RAG answer good?" "does my LLM app pass these tests?" "which prompt or model is best?" Runs your agent yes, many times per question, with timeouts and concurrency no: scores records you give it partly, through its test runner yes, prompts against providers Traces every step yes: model and tool calls, tokens, errors no through its tracing no Failures labelled by cause yes: tool error, timeout, rate limit, quota... no no no Metrics deterministic first (exact match, tool use, faithfulness, retrieval recall), LLM judge on top mostly LLM-based mostly LLM-based assertions, some LLM-based Judge calibrated against your labels yes, with Cohen's kappa no no no Says whether a change is real yes: paired McNemar test and confidence intervals no no side-by-side scores Blocks a PR on a regression yes: gate and GitHub Action no through test failures through assertions Interface CLI, Python, dashboard Python Python, cloud platform CLI, web viewer

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
• agenteval when an agent calls tools, runs in production, and you need to know why it fails and whether a change helps, not only how good one answer is.
  • Ragas when you want its catalogue of LLM-judged RAG metrics. They work together: agenteval export --format ragas turns a run into Ragas samples, and agenteval import reads Ragas samples back.
  • DeepEval when you want evaluations written as pytest-style unit tests with a hosted platform around them.
  • promptfoo when the job is comparing prompts and models across providers in a matrix.

docs.title: What agenteval doesn't do
docs.text:
• Simulated users: a conversation's user turns are written in the dataset, not generated in reply to the agent.
  • Hosting: it runs on your machine or your server; there is no managed service.
  • Tracing frameworks other than OpenAI and Anthropic clients and LangChain/LangGraph automatically; others are traced by wrapping their calls with llm_call and tool, or imported from their OpenTelemetry traces.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Concept What it is Case One question, its expected answer, and optionally the tools it needs, its category, text the answer must never contain, and the documents it is answered from. Trial One attempt at one case. Each case runs several times (--attempts, 3 by default), because LLMs don't answer the same way every time. Span (step) One model call or tool call inside a trial: start and end time, tokens, status, error type and message, and for tools the arguments and result. Score A judgement about a trial by one scorer, from 0 to 1, with its reasoning. Scores are stored apart from trials, so scorers can be fixed or added and re-run without calling the model again (agenteval rescore). Experiment One run of one agent configuration over one dataset: its trials, scores, prices at the time, status and the environment it ran in. Version A hash of the agent's configuration (model, prompt, parameters, and for your own agent the hash of its source file). Any change gives a new version, so comparisons know what changed.

docs.title: What happens in a run
docs.text:
1. The runner starts each trial (case × attempt) with a timeout, a few at a time (--concurrency).
  2. Your agent answers. Every llm_call and tool becomes a span.
  3. When a trial finishes, the scorers judge it, and the trial and its scores are saved at once. A run cut short keeps everything already done and can be resumed with --resume.
  4. If the trial ended on an exception, it gets a failure type from the step that raised: tool_error, llm_error, timeout, timeout_after_rate_limit, quota_exhausted, max_steps_exceeded, output_truncated, empty_output, invalid_model_output.

docs.title: Failures vs wrong answers
docs.text: A failure stopped the trial: it never produced an answer. A wrong answer finished but didn't match the expected one. They need different fixes (infrastructure and error handling vs the model, prompt or tools), so reports and the dashboard always show them apart.

docs.title: Infrastructure vs model
docs.text: A rate limit or an exhausted daily quota says something about the API that day, not about the agent. agenteval labels them separately, and the gate refuses to judge a change when more than 10% of trials failed for infrastructure reasons.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Why run each question several times? LLMs don't answer the same way every time, even at temperature 0. One attempt per question mistakes luck for quality. Three is the default; use an odd number so a case can't tie.

The comparison says "Inconclusive". Is the change safe? Not necessarily: it means a drop of that size can't be told apart from chance with this many cases. agenteval power shows how many cases you'd need. The gate can block Inconclusive results with --block-inconclusive.

Why does a right answer fail tool_selection or tool_faithfulness? Because it wasn't backed by the tools: the model answered from memory or worked it out in its head. In an agent that's a risk even when the answer happens to be right.

A run stopped halfway (Ctrl+C, a crash, the quota). Is it lost? No. Every finished trial is saved as it finishes. Run the same command with --resume <experiment id>; only the missing trials run.

Most trials failed with quota_exhausted or rate_limit. That's the provider, not your agent. Reports and comparisons label these as infrastructure failures, and the gate won't judge a run where over 10% of trials failed this way. Use --rpm/--tpm to stay under limits, --max-cost to cap spending, and run again after the quota resets.

My model isn't in the price table. agenteval prices --update, or pass --price INPUT OUTPUT (dollars per million tokens).

Can the LLM judge be trusted? Only as far as you've checked it: label about 50 answers (agenteval calibrate label, or the dashboard) and look at the kappa. Below 0.6, read its scores as leads, not measurements.

Does it work in Jupyter? Yes: evaluate() works inside a running event loop, and Results displays as an HTML report.

Does agenteval send my data anywhere? No telemetry. Only the calls you configure (your agent, the judge, generate) send data to their providers. See Privacy.

Why is it pip install pyagenteval but import agenteval? agenteval was taken on PyPI, so the package follows the common "py" + import name convention, as pyyaml gives import yaml. Version 1.0.0 was published as zeustucz-agenteval; install pyagenteval instead.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install "pyagenteval[server]"

Python 3.11 or newer. [server] adds the dashboard; leave it out for the command line and Python API only. Other extras: [gemini] for Google's SDK, [rag] for the RAG dataset's search index, [all] for everything.

docs.title: 2. Start a project
docs.text:
mkdir my-eval && cd my-eval
agenteval init

This writes three files:

File What it is my_agent.py an example agent: a function that takes a question and returns an answer cases.jsonl four questions with their expected answers agenteval.toml which agent, model, price and dataset agenteval run uses

To start from an agent closer to yours, pick a template: agenteval init --template openai (or anthropic, langgraph, rag). Each writes a working agent and its cases, and says what to install and which key to set.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
agenteval run
agenteval report

The example needs no API key: its "model" is a few lines of rules. The report shows the pass rate, every check, latency, cost and failures.

docs.title: 4. Put in your own agent
docs.text:
Replace the body of answer in my_agent.py with your agent. Wrap model calls in llm_call and tool calls in tool, so each becomes a step agenteval can time, price and score:

from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from agenteval import llm_call, tool

client = AsyncOpenAI()

async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    with llm_call("gpt-4o-mini") as call:
        response = await client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
        call.tokens(response.usage.prompt_tokens, response.usage.completion_tokens)
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Using an OpenAI client? wrap_openai(client) records every call for you; LangChain and LangGraph have a callback. See Connect your agent.

Then set the model and its price in agenteval.toml:

[run]
agent = "my_agent:answer"
model = "gpt-4o-mini"
price = [0.15, 0.60]   # dollars per million input and output tokens

agenteval prices --update fetches current prices for thousands of models, after which price can usually be left out.

docs.title: 5. Write your questions
docs.text:
One JSON object per line in cases.jsonl. Only input and expected_output are required:

{"input": "What is our refund window?", "expected_output": "30 days", "category": "policy"}

No questions yet? agenteval generate docs/ writes them from your documents. See Write a dataset.

docs.title: 6. Look, change, compare
docs.text:
agenteval ui                 # browse runs, open failures, compare two runs
agenteval compare 1 2        # is run 2 really better than run 1?

From Python or a notebook instead:

from agenteval import evaluate
results = evaluate(answer, "cases.jsonl", model="gpt-4o-mini", price=(0.15, 0.60))
results            # the report (an HTML table in Jupyter)
results.failures() # the trials that didn't pass, with question and answer

docs.title: Results from real runs
docs.text:
Runs 2 to 5 use the same 16-question dataset: large calculations, capital cities the model already knows, and one country missing from the tool's database, where the honest answer is "unknown".

Run Model Result What it showed 2 gemini-2.5-flash 11/11 completed trials correct; 5 failed Every failure was a 429, not the model. Inspecting individual trials found a bug in my own scorer: tool_selection reported 81% because trials that never got a response counted as "wrong tool". Fixed and re-scored to 100%. 3 gemini-2.5-flash 1/16 Requests rejected at about 2 per minute, far under the per-minute limit, which pointed to the daily quota. The failures were mislabelled timeout and wasted 15 minutes. Led to error messages on spans, cause-specific timeout labels and the circuit breaker. 4 gemini-2.5-flash 0/16 in under 1 s The circuit breaker worked on a real error. The stored message showed the free tier allows 20 requests/day, fewer than one run of the dataset needs. 5 openai/gpt-oss-20b (Groq) 48/48 Correct tool every time, said "unknown" for the missing country, about 1 s per question, about 6.5× cheaper per success than Gemini at paid-tier prices. The one retry was on a tokens-per-minute limit, not requests. 6 openai/gpt-oss-20b (Groq), hard dataset 49/55 (89.1%) The hard dataset separated the categories. Prompt injection succeeded 2 of 4 times, and my own system prompt caused the no_tool failures: its "reply unknown" rule made the model refuse "spell 'dog' backwards". 7, 8 Old vs new prompt, hard dataset, run side by side 87.3% vs 88.2%, Inconclusive The fix worked where it was aimed (no_tool 67% to 100%, with ambiguous staying at 100%), but long_chain fell from 67% to 42%, so the total barely moved. Recorded tool arguments showed the model doing sums in its head, and once calling 21021 + 0 after working out the answer itself.

Lessons:

  • Read individual trials, not just the summary. The summary hid a scorer bug.
  • A comparison only means something if only one thing changed. Runs 2 and 3 differed in quota as well as settings, so they can't be compared.
  • Separate infrastructure failures from model failures. "68.8% correct" and "100% correct, 31% blocked by rate limits" lead to completely different fixes.
  • An average can hide large moves in both directions. Runs 7 and 8 differ by 0.9 points overall, while four categories moved by 12 to 33 points.
  • A fix can work and still not be provable. With 55 cases and 3 attempts, even a 15-point drop is caught only about half the time.
  • Test the gate on a known-bad change. The first demonstration let a 23.6-point drop through, because tied cases counted as improvements and pushed p to 0.052. Measuring detection rates then showed my claim that 55 cases catch 10-point changes was wrong.
  • The total-vs-working latency gap in run 5 (57.8 s vs 1.6 s at p95) is my own rate limiter. It allowed 25 requests in any 60 s window, so it sent bursts and then waited. It now spaces requests evenly and can also respect a token limit.

docs.title: What a comparison can detect
docs.text:
"Inconclusive" doesn't mean "no change". This table shows how often a real drop was detected, from 100 mock comparisons for each cell:

Cases Attempts 5-point drop 10-point 15-point 25-point 55 2 0% 0% 5% 35% 55 3 3% 19% 50% 93% 200 2 3% 31% 75% 100% 500 2 27% 82% 99% 100%

Use an odd number of attempts, and more cases to catch smaller drops. The mock's faults are random on every attempt. Real regressions are often consistent, as with the damaged prompt below, so these figures are a cautious guide rather than exact rates for a real model.

Recompute this for your own pass rate and attempts with agenteval power.

docs.title: Compare versions and gate CI
docs.text:
A "version" is any change to the agent: its prompt, model, settings, tools or code. agenteval compare answers one question: is B really better than A, or did it get lucky?

agenteval run --name before ...
# change the agent
agenteval run --name after ...
agenteval compare 1 2

Differs in:   prompt

Pass rate:    87.3% -> 88.2%   +0.9 points   95% CI [-9.1, +10.9]
McNemar:      3 improved, 3 regressed   p = 1.000   (7 more changed only partly)
Latency:      1663ms -> 1548ms per trial, excluding waits   -115ms   95% CI [-301, +72]

Categories that moved (leads to investigate, not proof):
  long_chain        66.7% -> 41.7%  (6 cases)
  no_tool           66.7% -> 100.0%  (6 cases)

Verdict: Inconclusive. this could be chance: the true change is plausibly between -9 and +11 points.

In the dashboard, tick two experiments in the list and press Compare. In Python, after.compare(before).

docs.title: How it decides
docs.text:
• Fairness first. Different datasets are refused (a content hash catches an edited dataset), and so is an interrupted run. It warns if more than one setting changed, if attempts differ, if the runs are over 24 hours apart, or if infrastructure failures distorted a run.
  • Paired, case by case. Both versions answer the same questions, which removes differences in how hard each question is.
  • McNemar's exact test on the cases that cleanly flipped. A case that ties (1 of 2 attempts) has no majority, so it isn't counted as a flip: use an odd number of attempts.
  • Bootstrap confidence intervals resample cases, not trials, because attempts at the same question aren't independent.
  • Four verdicts: Better, Worse, Trade-off (better, but with new safety failures or meaningfully slower or costlier) and Inconclusive, which means "couldn't tell", not "they're the same". agenteval power tells you how many cases you need to tell.

docs.title: Gate pull requests
docs.text:
agenteval gate baseline.db candidate.db turns a comparison into an exit code CI acts on:

Result Exit code Better, Inconclusive, or better but slower or costlier (pass, with a warning) 0 Worse, or any new safety failure 1 Different datasets, an interrupted run, or over 10% infrastructure failures (can't judge) 2

Stricter options: --block-inconclusive (small drops can hide in Inconclusive) and --min-pass-rate 0.85.

docs.title: With the GitHub Action
docs.text:
Run your agent on the pull request, download a baseline database saved from main, then:

- uses: ZeusTucZ/agent-eval@v1
  with:
    baseline-db: baseline.db
    candidate-db: candidate.db
    block-inconclusive: "false"

The job fails on a block or can't-judge, and the Markdown report goes to the job summary (and to steps.<id>.outputs.report, to post as a PR comment).

docs.title: Budgeting CI runs
docs.text: A run of the agent costs tokens, and free tiers are small: on Groq's, one 55-case run with 3 attempts uses about 140,000 of the 200,000 tokens allowed per day. This repository's own workflows therefore run the gate only on pull requests labelled run-agent-eval, and store the main baseline once instead of re-running it for every pull request. Copy them from .github/workflows/agent-eval*.yml. For a cheaper check on every pull request, gate on a fixed --sample of the dataset, run the same way for the baseline.

docs.title: Know the price
docs.text:
Cost is tokens × a price table, in dollars per million tokens.

agenteval prices              # the table in use, and how old it is
agenteval prices gpt-4o       # search it
agenteval prices --update     # fetch current prices for thousands of models

--update downloads the list LiteLLM maintains and saves it to ~/.agenteval/prices.json (or AGENTEVAL_PRICES_FILE), which takes precedence over the built-in table. For a model that isn't listed, pass --price INPUT OUTPUT to run or judge, or price=(input, output) to evaluate; 0 0 if you don't track cost. A run refuses to start without a price for its --model rather than report a misleading $0. A different model your agent calls that has no price is recorded at $0 with a warning.

Each experiment keeps a snapshot of the prices it ran with, so later updates don't rewrite history.

docs.title: Before a run
docs.text:
agenteval estimate --model gpt-4o-mini --dataset cases.jsonl --attempts 3

Estimates cost and time from earlier runs of the same model (same dataset preferred). With no history, it suggests a 5-case pilot: agenteval run ... --sample 5 --attempts 1.

docs.title: During a run
docs.text:
agenteval run ... --max-cost 2.50

Stops starting new trials once $2.50 has been spent; trials already running finish and are saved. Continue later with the same options, --resume <id> and a higher --max-cost.

docs.title: Spend less
docs.text:
• --sample N runs N cases, spread across categories: the same N every time, so sampled runs compare with each other.
  • Fewer attempts while iterating, more (and odd) when it matters.
  • agenteval rescore re-runs the scorers on saved trials without calling the model.
  • A response cache (wrap_openai(client, cache="cache.db"), same for wrap_anthropic) replays identical requests from a file, so re-running an unchanged agent is free.
  • The judge's cache makes re-judging the same answers free; --sample judges a subset.
  • Rate limits: --rpm spaces requests evenly and --tpm respects a tokens-per-minute cap, so you aren't paying in retries for 429s.

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text:
pip install "pyagenteval[server]"
agenteval ui

Opens your browser on http://127.0.0.1:8765 with the experiments in agenteval.db (--db for another). It listens on this machine only, and a token for the session is made up and handed to the browser, so actions work without typing one.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Experiments, newest first, with pass rate, latency, cost and age. Interrupted runs are marked. Tick two to compare them.
  • An experiment, ordered by what you want to know: four headline numbers; why trials didn't pass (failures and wrong answers, largest first); search or answer, for RAG runs; pass rate by category; every check, the judge's and your own scorers; then the trials, opened on the ones that didn't pass, each with its question, expected answer, answer, steps and scores with their reasoning; for conversations, the whole exchange. Below the headline, the pass rate of every run of the same model on the same dataset, oldest first, with a link to compare this run with the one before.
  • A comparison: the verdict in plain words, the change with its confidence interval, categories that moved, and the questions that flipped, with both answers.
  • Label answers: one answer at a time, p or f, to check the LLM judge; the agreement appears once both exist.
  • New run: the built-in agents and datasets. Your own agents run from the command line.

Every view has its own link (#/e/3, #/compare/1/2), so you can share them.

docs.title: Deploying it
docs.text:
agenteval ui is for your own machine. To publish results:

  • One service: build the dashboard into the package (cd dashboard && npm ci && npm run build, then copy dashboard/dist to agenteval/static), and run uvicorn agenteval.api:app. It serves the API and the dashboard together.
  • Separately: deploy dashboard/ as a static site with VITE_API_URL set to the API's address, and add the site's address to the API's CORS_ORIGINS.

For a public demo, set READ_ONLY=1: every change (runs, re-scoring, labels, deletes) is refused whatever the token. With DEMO_SEED=1 an empty database starts with three example runs of the mock agent, so a demo on a disk that's wiped at each deploy isn't empty. Otherwise set API_TOKEN and keep it secret; the API also limits each client to REQUESTS_PER_CLIENT_PER_MINUTE (120 by default). The repository's Dockerfile and render.yaml deploy the API on Render.

docs.title: Write a dataset
docs.text:
A dataset is a JSONL file: one case per line.

{"input": "What is the refund window?", "expected_output": "30 days", "category": "policy"}
{"input": "Convert 100 EUR to USD.", "expected_output": "108.70", "expected_tools": ["convert_currency"]}
{"input": "Who is our CFO?", "expected_output": "unknown", "category": "unanswerable"}
Field Required Meaning input yes, unless turns the question expected_output yes the right answer; "" for none (exact match is then skipped) id no defaults to the line number; must be unique category no kind of question; reports break the pass rate down by it expected_tools no tools the agent must call, repeated once per call needed; [] means it must call none must_not_contain no text the answer must never include, e.g. an injected instruction's payload expects_tool_error no the tool is meant to fail here; how the agent handles it is what's tested relevant_docs no ids of the documents holding the answer, for retrieval recall; [] for none expected_trajectory no tool names in the order they should be called, for trajectory_order max_tool_calls no how many tool calls the task needs, for step_efficiency turns no a conversation: the user's messages in order (see below)

Errors in the file name the line they're on.

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text:
{"turns": ["I want to return my order.", "It's order 1234, bought 40 days ago."],
 "expected_output": "not eligible", "category": "refunds"}

The agent answers each turn in turn (how it gets them); the answer to the last one is checked against expected_output, and must_not_contain is checked against every reply. input defaults to the last turn.

docs.title: How many cases?
docs.text:
More than you'd think. With 55 cases and 3 attempts, a 10-point drop is caught only about a fifth of the time. Check before you trust a comparison:

agenteval power --pass-rate 0.85 --attempts 3

Use an odd number of attempts (ties can't count as a change), and cover each category with several cases.

docs.title: Generate cases from your documents
docs.text:
agenteval generate docs/ -n 50 -o cases.jsonl --corpus-out corpus.jsonl

Splits .md and .txt files into passages, and asks a model for one question per passage whose short answer is stated in it, linked by relevant_docs. About 10% are questions the documents don't answer, expecting unknown (--unanswerable). Read the questions before relying on them: drop any whose answer is wrong or ambiguous.

docs.title: Quick runs on a sample
docs.text:
agenteval run --dataset cases.jsonl --sample 20

20 cases spread across categories, the same 20 every time for the same --sample-seed, so two sampled runs can be compared.

docs.title: The built-in datasets
docs.text: Name Cases Use arithmetic --cases N the mock agent; validating the harness mixed 16 real models: calculations, capitals, one missing country hard 55 in 10 categories planted errors, prompt injection, ambiguity, tool errors extended 200 in 11 categories the same tools as hard, enough cases to catch drops of about 10 points rag 45 in 6 categories search over a fictional company's documents ([rag] extra)

docs.title: Score traces you already have
docs.text:
When you can't or don't want agenteval to run your agent (production logs, another framework's traces), import what it did:

agenteval import traces.jsonl --model gpt-4o-mini
agenteval report
agenteval judge 1 --rubric answer_relevance

One record per line, in agenteval's form:

{"input": "What is our refund window?", "output": "30 days", "expected_output": "30 days",
 "category": "policy",
 "steps": [{"kind": "llm", "name": "gpt-4o-mini", "input_tokens": 812, "output_tokens": 40, "duration_ms": 950},
           {"kind": "tool", "name": "search", "input": {"q": "refunds"}, "output": ["..."], "duration_ms": 120}]}

or as a Ragas sample:

{"user_input": "What is our refund window?", "response": "30 days",
 "retrieved_contexts": ["Refunds are accepted within 30 days."], "reference": "30 days"}

Only the question and the answer are required. retrieved_contexts become a retrieve step, so groundedness and context relevance can be judged on them. Without an expected answer, exact match is skipped rather than failed: the reference-free judge rubrics (answer_relevance, context_relevance, groundedness) still apply. Records with the same question are grouped as attempts at one case. The questions are written next to the traces (traces.cases.jsonl) so reports can show them.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
Traces exported as OTLP JSON (a collector's file exporter, or Phoenix and Langfuse exports) import the same way; the format is detected, or force it with --format otlp:

agenteval import spans.json --model gpt-4o-mini

Each trace becomes one trial. Model and tool spans are recognized by the OpenInference conventions (openinference.span.kind, llm.token_count.*, tool.name, as written by Arize's instrumentors) or OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions (gen_ai.*). The question and answer come from the root span's input.value and output.value, or agenteval.input and agenteval.output if you set them yourself. There are no expected answers in traces, so exact match is skipped; tool checks, faithfulness and the judge still apply.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
agenteval export 3 -o trials.jsonl                 # agenteval's form: imports back as-is
agenteval export 3 --format ragas -o samples.jsonl # Ragas SingleTurnSample fields

The Ragas export lets you run Ragas's own metrics on runs made here, alongside agenteval's.

docs.title: LLM judge and calibration
docs.text:
Some answers can't be scored by matching strings. agenteval judge asks a second model for a pass or fail verdict on each answer of a saved experiment.

agenteval judge 12 --rubric groundedness
  • Model and provider: llama-3.3-70b-versatile on Groq by default. --provider openai, --provider openrouter (which reaches Anthropic, Google and many others), --provider ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with --base-url and --api-key-env. A different, larger model than the agent's is the usual choice.
  • Cost: --sample 100 judges a fixed random sample. Verdicts are cached by the exact request, so judging the same answers again costs nothing (--no-cache to ask anyway).
  • Prompt injection: the judge is told that everything it evaluates is data, not instructions. That matters when sources contain injected text.
  • Your own rubric, from a TOML file:
name = "politeness"
question = "Is the ANSWER polite to the user? Fail if it is curt or condescending."
uses_expected = false
uses_sources = false

agenteval judge 12 --rubric politeness.toml

Scores are stored as judge_<rubric>, tagged with a hash of the judge's model and prompt. agenteval rescore never deletes them.

docs.title: Check the judge before trusting it
docs.text:
A judge is a model too. Its pass rate means nothing until you know how often it agrees with a person. Label a fixed random sample yourself, without seeing its verdicts:

agenteval calibrate label 12 --rubric groundedness --sample 50

or in the dashboard: an experiment's Label answers page, with p and f as shortcuts. Then:

agenteval calibrate agree 12 --rubric groundedness

Trials compared:  50
Agreement:        88.0%
Cohen's kappa:    0.74  substantial agreement: usable for comparing versions, but read its failures
Pass rate:        human 64.0%, judge 70.0%

Cohen's kappa is agreement beyond chance: a judge that passes everything agrees 90% of the time with labels that are 90% passes, and gets a kappa of 0. Read the listed disagreements: they show what to fix in the rubric. Labels are saved in the experiment's database; --export labels.jsonl keeps a copy next to your dataset.

docs.title: What gets measured
docs.text: Every trial is scored by these, when they apply. A scorer that doesn't apply (no expected tools, no documents) gives no score rather than a misleading 0.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text:
exact_match: the answer equals the expected one, forgiving case, accents, surrounding space and a final period. Numbers compare by value, within 0.01 (19753.0 = 19,753). Skipped when the case has no expected answer.

For open-ended answers, where wording varies, use the LLM judge's correctness rubric.

docs.title: Tool use, step by step
docs.text:
Each rung fails for a different reason, so each has its own score:

  1. tool_selection: the agent called every tool the case needs, as often as needed. Answering from memory fails this even when the answer is right. Not judged when the model never responded (that's infrastructure, not a choice).
  2. tool_arguments_valid: every call named a real tool with valid arguments.
  3. tool_execution: every call with valid arguments ran without an error.

And how the agent got there:

  • trajectory_order: the tools in expected_trajectory were called in that order. Other calls in between are allowed; the order of the expected ones isn't negotiable.
  • step_efficiency: calls needed over calls made, at most 1. "Needed" is max_tool_calls, else the length of expected_trajectory or expected_tools. An agent that takes 6 calls for a 3-call task scores 0.5.
  • redundant_calls: fails when the same tool is called with the same arguments after it already worked. Retrying a call that failed is fine.

docs.title: Faithfulness and retrieval
docs.text:
• tool_faithfulness: every number in the answer, or its text, appears in a tool result. A deterministic hallucination check: it needs no reference and no LLM. It measures faithfulness to sources, not truth: a right answer worked out in the model's head fails it.
  • retrieval_recall: the share of the case's relevant_docs that any search returned. Crossed with exact_match, reports say whether a wrong answer came from the search (a document was missed) or from the model (it had them all).

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: avoids_forbidden_text: the answer contains none of the case's must_not_contain, such as an injected instruction's payload. The gate blocks any new failure here whatever else improved.

docs.title: Latency, cost and failures
docs.text:
• Latency p50/p95, both total (what a user waits) and excluding waits (time inside requests, without retries and rate limiting).
  • Cost: tokens × the price table, total and per correct answer.
  • Retries by reason, and failures by cause (see Concepts).

docs.title: LLM judge rubrics
docs.text:
Scored by a second model with agenteval judge; see LLM judge.

Rubric Question Needs correctness same answer as expected, whatever the wording? expected answer groundedness every claim supported by the tool results? tool results answer_relevance does it address the question asked? nothing context_relevance do the retrieved sources contain what's needed? tool results

docs.title: Your own scorers
docs.text:
A function of (case, trial) returning a number from 0 to 1, a bool, a (value, reason) pair, a Score, or None to skip:

def concise(case, trial):
    return len(trial.output or "") < 200, "under 200 characters"

agenteval run ... --scorer my_scorers:concise

or evaluate(..., scorers=[concise]). Its scores appear under "Other scores", and agenteval rescore runs it again.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text: Every experiment is a SQLite file on your machine (agenteval.db by default). It holds each question, answer, tool argument, tool result and error message, up to a length per field. Nothing is sent anywhere by agenteval itself: there is no telemetry.

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text:
• Your agent's calls go wherever your agent sends them, as they would without agenteval.
  • The LLM judge sends the question, answer and, for some rubrics, the tool results and expected answer to the judge's provider. Use a provider you're allowed to share that data with, or a local model (--provider ollama).
  • agenteval generate sends passages of your documents to the model you choose.
  • agenteval prices --update downloads a public price list; it sends nothing.

docs.title: Keeping personal data out of the database
docs.text:
agenteval run ... --redact

replaces emails, phone and card numbers, IBANs, IP addresses and API keys with markers like [EMAIL] before anything is saved. Scores are computed first, from the real text, so a correct answer that contains an email still counts as correct. evaluate(..., redact=True) does the same from Python. Account ids in provider error messages (org_...) are always removed, since databases end up in CI artifacts.

Redaction is pattern-based: it catches common formats, not names or free-text secrets. For sensitive data, run on synthetic or anonymised cases, and keep databases out of public places.

docs.title: Reporting a security problem
docs.text: See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Connect your agent
docs.text: Your agent stays your code. agenteval needs two things from it: a way to call it with a question, and to know which model calls and tool calls it made. Pick whichever fits.

docs.title: A function, with steps wrapped by hand
docs.text:
from agenteval import llm_call, tool, ToolArgumentError

async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    with llm_call("gpt-4o-mini") as call:
        response = await client.chat.completions.create(...)
        call.tokens(response.usage.prompt_tokens, response.usage.completion_tokens)

    weather = await tool("get_weather", get_weather, city="Lisbon")
    ...
    return final_answer
  • The function may be sync or async. Sync agents run in a thread, so they don't block each other; a timeout can't stop a hung thread, though, so prefer async if steps can hang.
  • A parameter named case receives the whole case (with its category and expected tools) instead of the question.
  • llm_call(model) records one model request. Report its tokens with call.tokens(...) so cost can be counted. Before re-raising an error, call.failed_because("rate_limit") labels it by cause rather than exception class.
  • tool(name, function, *args, **kwargs) calls a sync or async tool and records its arguments and result, or its error. Raise ToolArgumentError for arguments the tool can't accept: that's scored as the agent's bad call, not the tool's failure.
  • Outside an evaluation both helpers just run what they wrap: the agent works normally.

docs.title: An OpenAI client, recorded automatically
docs.text:
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from agenteval import wrap_openai

client = wrap_openai(AsyncOpenAI())  # or OpenAI(); any compatible base_url works

Every client.chat.completions.create(...) becomes a model step named after its model, with the tokens the response reports. Works with Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM, Azure and anything else behind the OpenAI SDK. Tools still go through tool(...).

docs.title: An Anthropic client, recorded automatically
docs.text:
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
from agenteval import wrap_anthropic

client = wrap_anthropic(AsyncAnthropic())  # or Anthropic()

Every client.messages.create(...) becomes a model step, its input tokens including any read from or written to the prompt cache.

docs.title: Replay responses instead of paying again
docs.text:
Both wrappers take a cache:

client = wrap_openai(AsyncOpenAI(), cache=".agenteval-cache.db")

A request identical to one already made in the same attempt is answered from the file, instantly and with no tokens. Re-running an experiment while you tune scorers, a judge or the report then costs nothing; change the prompt or the model and the requests differ, so they go to the API. Each attempt has its own entries, so attempts stay independent.

docs.title: LangChain and LangGraph
docs.text:
from agenteval.integrations.langchain import AgentEvalCallback

async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    result = await graph.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", question)]},
                                 config={"callbacks": [AgentEvalCallback()]})
    return result["messages"][-1].content

Needs langchain-core. Every chat model call becomes a model step (with the tokens LangChain reports) and every tool call a tool step.

docs.title: Conversations
docs.text:
A case with turns is a conversation (see datasets). Give your function a parameter named messages and it gets the conversation so far, one call per user turn:

async def answer(messages: list[dict]) -> str:
    response = await client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=messages)
    return response.choices[0].message.content

messages is [{"role": "user" | "assistant", "content": ...}], ending with the newest user turn. Your replies are added to it, the last reply is the answer that's scored, and the whole transcript is saved and shown in reports, the dashboard and to the LLM judge.

docs.title: An object with a run method
docs.text: The built-in agents implement async def run(self, case, attempt, tracer) -> str. An object with that method can be passed directly, for full control over the trace.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Command linePython 
agenteval run --agent my_project.agents:answer --model gpt-4o-mini --price 0.15 0.60 \
    --dataset cases.jsonl

from agenteval import evaluate
results = evaluate(answer, "cases.jsonl", model="gpt-4o-mini", price=(0.15, 0.60))

--model names the model llm_call uses when it isn't given one, and prices it. A hash of the agent's source file becomes part of its version, so two versions of your code can be compared even when the model and prompt are the same.

docs.title: The built-in agents
docs.text: --agent groq, --agent gemini and --agent mock (fault-injecting, for testing the harness) are tool-calling agents you can run on the built-in datasets with no code at all. examples/groq_agent.py in the repository is a real tool-calling agent to copy from.

real agents (gemini, groq):

docs.title: agenteval.toml
docs.text:
Options for every command can live in agenteval.toml in the directory you run from, so a project's runs need no long command lines. agenteval init writes one.

# Applies to every command that has a --db option.
db = "results/agenteval.db"

[run]
agent = "my_project.agents:answer"
model = "gpt-4o-mini"
price = [0.15, 0.60]          # a list for options that take several values
dataset = "cases.jsonl"
attempts = 3
max_cost = 2.0
redact = true                 # true for flags; false or leaving it out for off
scorer = ["my_scorers:concise", "my_scorers:polite"]   # repeated options: a list

[judge]
model = "llama-3.3-70b-versatile"
provider = "groq"

[report]
format = "markdown"
  • Each table is named after a command, and each key is one of its options (see the command line reference) with - or _.
  • Anything on the command line wins over the file.
  • For calibrate, the [calibrate] options apply to both label and agree.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Used by GROQ_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY built-in agents, the judge, generate AGENTEVAL_PRICES_FILE where prices --update saves prices (default ~/.agenteval/prices.json) DATABASE_PATH the API server's database API_TOKEN the API server's token for changes (agenteval ui makes one up) READ_ONLY 1 refuses every change on the API server DEMO_SEED 1 fills an empty database with example runs when the API server starts CORS_ORIGINS sites allowed to call the API server from a browser REQUESTS_PER_CLIENT_PER_MINUTE the API server's per-client limit (120; 0 for none) AGENTEVAL_STATIC_DIR a built dashboard for the API server to serve at /

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from agenteval import (
    evaluate, aevaluate, Results,          # run and read results
    llm_call, tool, ToolArgumentError,     # trace your agent's steps
    wrap_openai, wrap_anthropic,           # trace an OpenAI or Anthropic client automatically
    as_scorer, Case, EvaluationCase,       # your own scorers and cases
)
from agenteval.integrations.langchain import AgentEvalCallback

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
results = evaluate(agent, cases, *, model, price=None, attempts=3, scorers=(), name="python-run",
                   db=None, concurrency=4, timeout=120.0, max_cost=None, sample=None,
                   redact=False, progress=False, config=None)
Argument Meaning agent a function taking the question (or a parameter named case) and returning the answer, sync or async; or an object with run(case, attempt, tracer) cases a .jsonl path, a built-in dataset name ("hard", "arithmetic-50"), or a list of dicts or Cases model the model llm_call uses by default, for pricing price (input, output) dollars per million tokens, if model isn't in the price table scorers functions of (case, trial), see as_scorer db save to this SQLite file like a CLI run; in memory when None max_cost stop starting trials once this much has been spent sample run this many cases, spread across categories redact replace personal data before saving config extra settings recorded in the version, e.g. {"prompt": PROMPT, "temperature": 0}

Works inside a running event loop (Jupyter) by running in its own thread. aevaluate is the async form, with the same arguments.

docs.text:
Member What it gives pass_rate exact-match pass rate, or None without expected answers cost total cost in dollars score("tool_selection") the mean of one scorer summary everything the report shows, as a dict report(fmt="text") the report: "text", "json", "markdown", "html" or "csv" save("report.html") write the report; the format follows the extension failures() the trials that didn't pass, with question, expected answer and answer to_records(), to_pandas() one row per trial with every score (pandas is optional) compare(baseline) is this run better than baseline, as agenteval compare check(min_pass_rate=, min_scores=, max_cost=, max_failures=) raise AssertionError listing what fell short; returns the results otherwise experiment, trials, scores, cases the raw objects

In Jupyter, a Results displays as the HTML report.

check turns an evaluation into a test:

def test_support_agent():
    evaluate(answer, "cases.jsonl", model="gpt-4o-mini", attempts=3).check(
        min_pass_rate=0.9, min_scores={"tool_selection": 1.0}, max_cost=0.50)

A failure names each limit missed and the first failing questions with their answers.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
with llm_call(model=None) as call:     # a model step; model defaults to evaluate's model
    ...
    call.tokens(input_tokens, output_tokens)
    call.failed_because("rate_limit")  # optional, before raising: label the error by cause

result = await tool(name, function, *args, **kwargs)  # a tool step; function sync or async

Raise ToolArgumentError inside a tool for arguments it can't accept. Outside an evaluation both helpers simply run what they wrap.

wrap_openai(client, cache=None) returns the client with chat.completions.create recorded (sync or async); wrap_anthropic(client, cache=None) does the same for messages.create. cache is a file path for replaying identical requests. AgentEvalCallback() goes in a LangChain or LangGraph config={"callbacks": [...]}.

docs.title: as_scorer
docs.text:
def concise(case, trial):                 # return 0..1, a bool, (value, reason), a Score or None
    return len(trial.output or "") < 200, "under 200 characters"

evaluate(agent, cases, model="m", scorers=[concise])
as_scorer(lambda case, trial: 0.5, name="half")   # name a lambda

A trial has output, failure_type, attempt, case_id and spans; each span has kind ("llm" or "tool"), name, status, input, output, error_type, tokens and times.
